messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Lawyer
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 71

She is 71, a South Eastern Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life working as a lawyer, the kind of attorney who is known for careful preparation, measured language, and the ability to stay composed in adversarial rooms. She has been married for decades. When she speaks about the assault, she does so in the same precise way she once used to summarize a case file, but the order of events keeps breaking apart on her. Certain details are painfully sharp; others disappear the moment she reaches for them.

The assault happens three years ago, on an early evening after she leaves her office. She has stayed late to review documents for a property dispute and is carrying a leather bag heavy with files. In the parking structure, she hears footsteps behind her but tells herself not to overreact. She has spent a lifetime moving through male-dominated spaces by appearing unshaken. Before she reaches her car, a man grabs her from behind, yanks her bag, and shoves her hard against a concrete pillar. She remembers the smell of engine oil, the scrape of her cheek, the shock more than the pain. He strikes her when she resists. She still cannot say with certainty how long it lasts. She remembers thinking, with a strange detached clarity, that no one is coming. By the time he runs, taking her bag, she is on the ground, one shoe off, her blouse torn at the shoulder.

In the hours afterward, she moves as if she is acting in someone else’s body. She gives a statement, calls her husband, answers questions from police officers who seem younger than her children. At home, she showers for a long time, then feels ashamed for washing away evidence, though the forensic exam has already been done. She does not sleep that night. Every time she closes her eyes, she is back in the parking garage, hearing footsteps quicken behind her. She gets up repeatedly to check the locks, then startles at the click of the deadbolt she herself has turned.

At first, she tells herself she will recover by discipline. She returns to work quickly, wearing a scarf to cover the bruising near her neck. In meetings she finds she can still argue statutes and timelines, but if someone walks too closely behind her chair, her whole body jerks. She begins arriving at the office only after sunrise and refuses to stay past late afternoon. She asks a junior associate to accompany her to the garage and tells him it is because of her age, because stairs are difficult now, though she takes the stairs briskly when alone at home. She changes parking lots three times in two months. The unpredictability of elevators, stairwells, and enclosed spaces starts to shape her days.

She is most unsettled by how the assault enters ordinary moments. The clatter of footsteps in a courthouse hallway makes her heart pound so hard she presses a hand to her chest and loses track of what opposing counsel is saying. A man reaching across her at a copy machine leaves her dizzy and trembling in the restroom. She avoids the garage where it happened, then avoids the entire neighborhood, then finds herself scanning every street, every stranger, every exit. Her husband notices that she no longer sits with her back to a restaurant door. At night she wakes gasping from dreams in which she cannot turn around fast enough. Sometimes in the dream she is old, sometimes young, but always helpless. When she wakes, she needs several minutes to remember which year she is in.

Before the assault, she prides herself on her memory and concentration. Now she reads the same paragraph in a brief four times without retaining it. She loses words in court and covers with irritation. She has become short-tempered with clerks and associates, then privately mortified by it. At home, small noises make her snap. She says she feels “contaminated by vigilance,” as if some inner alarm has fused into the on position. She used to enjoy evening walks with her husband; now she insists on staying inside once it is dark. If he is ten minutes late returning from the market, she imagines blood, pavement, sirens. She knows these thoughts are unreasonable and cannot stop them.

What troubles her most is the change in how she understands herself. She has built a life on competence, argument, and the belief that preparation offers protection. Since the assault, she feels betrayed by her own body and by the world she once navigated confidently. She keeps replaying what she wore, where she parked, whether she should have asked security to escort her. She hears herself making the same objections she would dismantle in a courtroom, yet the self-blame persists. In sessions, she sometimes pauses midsentence and stares toward the door when footsteps pass outside. Then she gathers herself, smooths her sleeve, and continues, embarrassed by the interruption. She says she is tired of living as if danger is always one step behind her, but that is still how every day feels.
